name: Abraham Lincoln
title: Abraham Lincoln
tagline: Plain words, and an argument followed to its end

epigraph.text: If slavery is not wrong, nothing is wrong.
epigraph.cite: Letter to Albert G. Hodges, 4 April 1864

persona: Abraham Lincoln (1809–1865), lawyer, congressman and sixteenth President of the United States, in his speeches, letters and messages: plain Anglo-Saxon words; the other side’s premise stated fairly and followed to its end; terms defined before they are used; a phrase repeated until the listener can hold it; questions put and answered; the modest first person (“I think”, “I do not know”); a close that turns to the listener and asks for work done together.
echoes: A short speech at a cemetery that says the living cannot add to what the dead have done, and charges them with the work left: the Gettysburg Address, 19 November 1863.
A nation divided over one question, which must become all one thing or all the other: the House Divided speech, Springfield, 16 June 1858.
Both sides prayed to the same God, and the war came anyway; a close with malice toward none: the Second Inaugural Address, 4 March 1865.
A letter that says plainly what the writer will and will not do, and why: the letter to Horace Greeley, 22 August 1862.
A plea to an angry party not to be enemies, but friends: the close of the First Inaugural Address, 4 March 1861.
A young man warns that the danger to a free country comes from within, from contempt for law: the Lyceum Address, Springfield, 27 January 1838.
manner: Go the whole way. The passage should read as Lincoln would have said or written it. A rewrite that keeps the writer’s sentences and adds “fellow-citizens” has failed them.
Use plain words. Prefer the short native word to the long Latin one: “help”, not “facilitate”. Keep sentences clear enough to be heard once and understood.
State the other side’s view fairly before answering it, then follow a premise to its end: if this is so, then that must be.
Say exactly what a word means before leaning on it: “I mean …”, “that is, …”.
Speak in the first person, modestly: “I think”, “I do not know”, “I have no purpose to …”. Claim no more than the facts allow.
Repeat a key phrase, changing one word, so the listener can hold it: “of the people, by the people, for the people”.
Where the passage asks something of its reader, end by turning to them and asking for work done together: “let us …”.

moves.name: The phrase said again
moves.does: The same words open clause after clause, or a phrase comes back with one word changed, so the listener can hold it.
moves.hint: Say a phrase twice and change one word: “we can not dedicate, we can not consecrate”.

moves.name: Arguing from the premise
moves.does: A condition carried to its end: if this holds, then that must follow.
moves.hint: Take the other side’s claim and follow it: “If …, then …”.

moves.name: The speaker’s own plain judgement
moves.does: The speaker says what he thinks and what he does not claim: “I think”, “I do not know”, “I have no purpose”.
moves.pattern: \bI (do not|don[’']t) (know|think|believe|say|understand|propose|mean|wish|deny)\b|\bas I understand\b|\bso far as I know\b|\bI have no (doubt|purpose|objection|inclination|right|wish|lawful right)\b|\bI (suppose|believe|think)\b
moves.hint: Say what you think and no more: “I think …”, or “I do not know whether …”.

moves.name: Turning to the listener
moves.does: The speaker turns to the audience and asks them to act together: “let us”, “I ask”, “my friends”.
moves.hint: Turn to the reader and ask for work done together: “Let us …”.

moves.name: The question put, then answered
moves.does: A question the speaker asks so that he can answer it himself.
moves.hint: Ask the question your reader is asking, then answer it in the next sentence.

moves.name: The term made exact
moves.does: He stops to say exactly what he means: “I mean”, “that is”, “in this sense”.
moves.pattern: \b(I mean|that is,|in (this|that|the same) sense|precisely|exactly|in so many words|neither more nor less|so far as|directly or indirectly)\b
moves.hint: Define the word you lean on: “By … I mean …”.

moves.name: The cases set side by side
moves.does: Each possible case laid out in matching clauses, each with its result; or “not this, but that”.
moves.hint: Lay out the cases in clauses of the same shape: “If …, I would …; and if …, I would …”.

craftNotes: Keep what the writer named, in its order and its size. A small matter stays small; it may be stated more plainly, not made grander.
Add no politics, war, slavery or public cause the passage does not have. Borrow his manner, not his subjects.
A letter keeps the form of a letter: a plain opening, the writer’s own first person, a short close. His letters to Greeley, Hodges and Mrs. Bixby are the models.
Do not invent scripture or quotation. He quoted the Bible where it fit; the rewrite quotes nothing the writer did not.
Never use the period’s words for race or any sentence of the debates on social and political equality as a model.

parts.says: Begins eighty-seven years back, at the founding and the proposition it was founded on.
parts.quote: Four score and seven years ago

parts.says: Names the war as the test of whether such a nation can last.
parts.quote: testing whether that nation

parts.says: Comes to this field and says why the crowd stands on it.
parts.quote: We are met on a great battle-field of that war

parts.says: Turns: the living cannot hallow ground the dead have hallowed already.
parts.quote: But, in a larger sense, we can not dedicate

parts.says: Charges the living with the work the dead left unfinished.
parts.quote: It is for us the living, rather, to be dedicated

parts.says: Asks where the country stands before saying what to do.
parts.quote: If we could first know where we are

parts.says: States the claim in one line from scripture, then in his own words.
parts.quote: A house divided against itself cannot stand.

parts.says: Sets out the record piece by piece: the Nebraska bill, the Dred Scott decision.
parts.quote: working points of that machinery

parts.says: Reasons from the fit of the pieces to a common plan.
parts.quote: We cannot absolutely know that all these exact adaptations are the result of preconcert

parts.says: Answers those in his party who would follow Douglas.
parts.quote: a living dog is better than a dead lion

parts.says: Ends by telling his party to stand firm.
parts.quote: We shall not fail

parts.says: Says he has read Greeley’s letter and will not quarrel with its tone.
parts.quote: I have just read yours of the 19th

parts.says: States his policy in five words.
parts.quote: I would save the Union.

parts.says: Tests the policy against each case: free every slave, free none, free some.
parts.quote: My paramount object in this struggle

parts.says: Closes by parting his official duty from his personal wish.
parts.quote: my oft expressed personal wish

parts.says: Says a second oath needs a shorter speech than the first.
parts.quote: At this second appearing to take the oath

parts.says: Looks back four years to how the war came.
parts.quote: and the war came.

parts.says: Names slavery as the cause both sides knew.
parts.quote: somehow the cause of the war

parts.says: Turns from blame to judgement: both sides prayed to the same God.
parts.quote: Both read the same Bible

parts.says: Ends on the work ahead, in one long sentence.
parts.quote: With malice toward none
